# FDG9093

> DO implement `IEnumerable<T>` to enable basic LINQ support.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.6.3 Supporting LINQ through IEnumerable&lt;T>.

## How it is checked

- Check: sdk (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: CA1010
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: draft

CA1010 reports a type that implements the non-generic IEnumerable, ICollection or IList without the generic counterpart; it honors api_surface, so the library profile checks externally visible types and the application profile all types (probe with SDK 10.0.402). Which other types are data sets that need LINQ support is a judgment, so coverage is partial. Adding the generic interface adds to the public API without changing a signature; CA1010 has no code fix. CA1010 is shared with FDG8034.

## From the book

Such basic support should be sufficient for most in-memory data sets. The basic LINQ support will use the extension methods on `IEnumerable<T>` provided in .NET. For example, simply define the methods as follows:

```csharp
public class RangeOfInt32s : IEnumerable<int> {
  public IEnumerator<int> GetEnumerator() {...}
  IEnumerator IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() {...}
}
```

Doing so allows for the following code, despite the fact that `RangeOfInt32s` did not implement a `Where` method:

```csharp
   var a = new RangeOfInt32s();
   var b = a.Where(x => x>10);
```

> **Rico Mariani:** Keep in mind that you’ll get your same enumeration semantics, and putting a LINQ façade on them does not make them execute any faster or use less memory.
